# **Drosophila-PN-Transience-Mechanisms**

# **Mechanisms and Parameters for Drosophila Projection Neuron Transients**

## **Direct Answer**

**ORN→PN short-term synaptic depression** is the most plausible central mechanism for step transients: while **untested** directly in DM4, synaptic depression is **established** biophysically at *Drosophila* ORN→PN synapses (VM7, VM2)1 and dynamically fitted across DM6, VM2, VM7, and DL5 (*f* \= 0.78, *τ* \= 893 ms)2, providing a \~0.9 s timescale compatible with suppressing sustained plateaus while passing new steps. **ORN rate-of-change encoding** is **established** upstream in Or59b, yet DM4 PNs fire more phasically than Or59b, indicating additional central sharpening3. **Presynaptic GABA\_A/GABA\_B inhibition** is **established** for lateral gain control (DM1) and **plausible** for transience (higher total ORN activity increases PN transience), though GABA-blockade effect sizes on transience were unretrieved2. **Postsynaptic LN pathways** are **plausible** in DM4 models5 yet **untested** experimentally; **intrinsic PN properties** remain **untested** for transience1. Strongest case against adding one mechanism: unpaired, differently dissected Or59b/DM4 preparations3, miscalibrated static DM4 Olsen constants4, and overlapping, non-identifiable timescales across glomeruli.

## **Experimental Mechanisms Producing PN Transience**

Ranked by strength of evidence, the opened literature yields four primary experimental studies in *Drosophila melanogaster*1, no verified primary experimental studies in other insects (such as locust or moth), and one computational circuit model5. No opened calcium-imaging study was retrieved; an unopened imaging search excerpt mentioning DM1 calcium dynamics (PMC6581506)6 and an unopened excerpt on synaptic vesicle release probability (PMC10209050)7 remain unverified and are excluded from conclusions.  
**Short-term synaptic depression (STD) at ORN→PN synapses** is biophysically established at *Drosophila* central synapses and is the leading central candidate for converting sustained ORN firing into transient PN responses, though its quantitative percentage contribution to DM4 step bursts remains unmeasured in the retrieved studies. In an explant antennal lobe preparation with acutely removed antennae, suction-electrode stimulation of the antennal nerve, and somatic whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in glomeruli VM7 and VM2, Kazama and Wilson (2008) showed that ORN→PN synapses have high release probability and exhibit strong short-term depression under strong stimulation, proposing STD as a partial explanation for nonlinear ORN-to-PN response transformation1. Extending synaptic measurements to dynamic *in vivo* sensory stimulation, Nagel, Hong, and Wilson (2015) combined *in vivo* whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from GFP-labeled PNs with extracellular sensillum recordings from ORNs across DM6, VM2, VM7, and DL5, fitting a simple synaptic depression model with a recovery time constant of 893 ms and per-spike factor *f* \= 0.782. While an \~0.9 s recovery constant naturally depresses sustained plateaus relative to novel step onsets, the extracted text did not contain the fraction of PN transience attributable specifically to STD or any DM4 recording2.  
**Presynaptic inhibition of ORN terminals (GABA\_A and GABA\_B)** is established for lateral gain control and plausibly shapes PN transience, although neither its kinetics nor its isolated effect size on transience were retrieved. Recording ORN and PN single/population units alongside antennal local field potentials (LFPs) across VM7, DL5, and DM1, Olsen, Bhandawat, and Wilson (2010) showed that co-applying GABA\_A and GABA\_B antagonists (5 µM picrotoxin plus 10 µM CGP54626) blocks lateral blend suppression by pentyl acetate and raises gain in DM1 (though not in VM7), and further reported that increasing total ORN activity makes PN responses more transient4. Nagel, Hong, and Wilson (2015) likewise applied 5 µM picrotoxin and 50 µM CGP54626 *in vivo* across DM6, VM2, VM7, and DL52, but quantitative changes in PN step transience under GABA blockade were unavailable in the extracted text.  
**ORN firing adaptation and rate-of-change encoding** provide part of the transient waveform before signals reach the antennal lobe, yet cannot account for all of the observed DM4 PN transience. Recording *in vivo* from female *Drosophila* with tungsten electrodes in single basiconic sensilla (Or59b OSNs) and saline-filled 7–10 MΩ glass electrodes attached via gentle suction to exposed somata (DM4 PNs) during 17 photoionization-detector (PID)-measured acetone waveforms, Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy (2015) established that Or59b OSNs already encode concentration rate of change3. Even so, DM4 PNs exhibit higher peak firing rates and markedly more phasic spiking than presynaptic Or59b OSNs, signaling both OSN spike rate and its rate of change3. Upstream ORN dynamics therefore help drive step-onset timing, while an additional central sharpening transformation operates between Or59b and DM43.  
**Intrinsic PN properties** and **postsynaptic lateral excitation or inhibition from local neurons (LNs)** lack experimental evidence as drivers of PN transience in the opened primary studies. Kazama and Wilson (2008) showed that unitary synaptic currents in VM7 and VM2 scale to compensate lower dendritic input resistance and equalize steady depolarization across glomeruli1, and Nagel, Hong, and Wilson (2015) modeled PNs purely as leaky passive integrators rather than adapting spike generators2. For postsynaptic LN circuitry, Olsen, Bhandawat, and Wilson (2010) tested presynaptic lateral inhibition rather than postsynaptic LN transience4, while Lazar, Liu, and Yeh (2023) modeled differential excitatory (Post-eLN) and inhibitory (Post-iLN) feedforward LN pathways alongside presynaptic Pre-LN inhibition to generate ON/OFF contrast-boosting transients in DM45. Experimental testing of Post-eLN or Post-iLN transience generation was not found in these searches.

### **Verbatim Quotes for Measured Parameters**

Every verified numerical parameter in the table above is anchored to the following verbatim source passages. From Nagel, Hong, and Wilson (2015): "f \= 0.78 and τ \= 893 ms" (from the fit of the simple synaptic depression model)2; "The parameter r governs the rate of depression and is equivalent to (1- f) in Equation 1, and τA is equivalent to τ in"2; and "picrotoxin (5 μM) and CGP54626 (50 μM)"2. From Olsen, Bhandawat, and Wilson (2010): "Exponent: 1.5 (chosen because it produced the best fit)."4; "Fitted Constant / Conversion factor: 190 mV · sec^2 / spikes" for Equation (5)4; "GABA receptor antagonists (5 μM picrotoxin \+ 10 μM CGP54626) increase the gain in DM1 but not VM7 (red)."4; "Picrotoxin (5 μM) and CGP54626 (10 μM) were applied together to block both GABA-A and GABA-B receptors (Olsen and Wilson, 2008)."4; and "With antagonists, the response to the blend is significantly different from the response in control saline, and not significantly different from the response to the private odor alone (p\<0.05 and p=0.18, paired t-tests)."4. Note a dimensional discrepancy in the extracted Equation (5)/(6) denominator of Olsen et al. (2010): dividing a sum of firing rates (normally spikes/s) by 190 mV·sec²/spikes does not yield mV algebraically, so the printed units of this constant should be verified against the published PDF before embedding in code.  
From Lazar, Liu, and Yeh (2023), the parameter specifications state: "consisting of 23 free parameters (denoted by the vector \\boldsymbol{\\theta})"5; "Parameter: \\sigma^L \= 0"5; "Parameter: \\sigma^{eL} \= 0"5; "A heuristic constraint caps the maximum normalized neurotransmitter concentration of x\_{ro}^{AxT} across time and channels to 0.8 to prevent model saturation."5; and "Evaluated via objective function J\_2(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}\_1) over more than 10^6 parameter set values"5. From Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy (2015), experimental preparation parameters state: "Female Drosophila melanogaster flies (2–5 days posteclosion)", "1 mg/ml collagenase (Type I) for 1–2 minutes", "borosilicate patch electrode (7–10 MΩ tip resistance)"3, and "Sample traces of 17 acetone odor concentration waveforms and their responses in Or59b OSNs and DM4 PNs."8.

## **Models Reproducing PN Transients**

Four mathematical models appeared in the opened sources: one steady-state baseline (Olsen, Bhandawat, and Wilson 2010\)4 and three dynamical models2. Crucially for software implementation, no complete rate-based differential equation with all fitted numerical constants mapping continuous ORN firing rates to transient DM4 PN firing rates was recovered verbatim across these searches: Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy's 2D linear–nonlinear (LN) rate equation and Nagel, Hong, and Wilson's Equations 1–2 were omitted from the extracted texts2, while Lazar, Liu, and Yeh's 2023 circuit operates on discrete OSN spike trains ![][image1] rather than firing rates and omits the downstream PN soma equation and fitted parameter values in the retrieved excerpt5.

In the context of your benchmark tests, these structural differences explain why neither baseline model captures the DM4 step bursts. The steady-state Olsen equation omits slow depressive or high-pass dynamics and uses constants calibrated on non-DM4 glomeruli4, which lets sustained drive remain at 107 Hz (29 Hz baseline) instead of relaxing toward \~45 Hz (7 Hz baseline). Conversely, Lazar, Liu, and Yeh's circuit imposes a heuristic 0.8 ceiling on normalized axon-terminal neurotransmitter concentration ![][image18] specifically to prevent saturation while fitting multi-channel affinity-scaled PSTHs across channels via ![][image19]5 rather than matching unscaled single-channel peak firing amplitudes (which helps explain why your run of the published example circuit topped out near \~70 Hz rather than 150–190 Hz).

## **Lazar Group Work on Or59b and DM4 Recordings**

Across the opened record, two papers from Aurel A. Lazar's group directly address Or59b/DM4 temporal encoding and contrast processing—**Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy (2015)** (eLife, PMID 25974217\)3 and **Lazar, Liu, and Yeh (2023)** (*PLOS Computational Biology*, PMID 37083547, revising the 2021/2022 bioRxiv preprint associated with AntennalLobeLLY22)5. Five additional Lazar-group works referencing Or59b, DM4, or acetone staircases appeared only in search snippets or citation lists without opened full-text extractions and are therefore flagged as unverified8.  
**Where the staircase data were recorded and first published:** Anmo J. Kim, Aurel A. Lazar, and Yevgeniy B. Slutskiy recorded the PID-calibrated acetone concentration waveforms, Or59b OSN sensillum spikes, and DM4 PN spikes in female *Drosophila melanogaster* (NP3062-GAL4; UAS-mCD8::GFP)3. Figure 2 of Lazar, Liu, and Yeh (2023) explicitly describes the acetone concentration waveform as "first published in \[35\]"22, where reference \[35\] in that article's bibliography is Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy (2015)3. Earlier unopened papers (Kim et al., 2011 and 2011b) are cited inside those papers for Or59b/Or7a spike-sorting code8 and earlier Or59b OSN acetone experiments19, while the paired Or59b OSN and DM4 PN dataset across 17 dynamic acetone waveforms traces to the 2015 *eLife* publication3.  
**Mechanisms, circuit configurations, and quantitative fit:** Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy (2015) did not isolate a synaptic or circuit mechanism; using a phenomenological 2D LN model of OSN firing rate and its temporal derivative, they concluded that DM4 PNs encode both OSN spike rate and rate of change, cascading with OSN rate encoding to signal odor **acceleration** and **rate of change** via higher-peak, more phasic firing3. Lazar, Liu, and Yeh (2023) instead modeled PN responses as a sum of a **concentration-invariant** semantic odor-identity component and two transient **ON/OFF contrast-boosting** components generated by Local Neuron Differential Divisive Normalization Processors (DNPs)5. They concluded that multi-channel **Pre-LN** presynaptic inhibition is essential for concentration-invariant identity recovery—with both **feedforward and feedback** Pre-LN architectures performing effectively—while differential temporal operators (x\_2, x\_3) in **Post-eLN** and **Post-iLN** pathways generate transient ON/OFF contrast5. Although their 23-parameter DNP-FF model was optimized via Latin Hypercube Sampling and Differential Evolution on ![][image19] over more than ![][image20] evaluations5, neither the best-fit numerical parameters nor the quantitative fit metrics (such as correlation or SNR values referenced in a figure caption23) were available in the retrieved text.

## **The Case Against**

Four lines of experimental and modelling evidence argue against grafting any single transient synaptic or circuit module onto the static Olsen framework to fit the DM4 staircase data.  
First, **the Or59b OSN and DM4 PN recordings are unpaired across separate flies and sharply different preparations**. In Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy (2015), Or59b OSNs were recorded extracellularly using tungsten electrodes inserted into intact basiconic sensilla, whereas DM4 PNs were recorded in separate flies after opening the head capsule under saline, digesting the perineural sheath with 1 mg/ml Type I collagenase for 1–2 minutes, rupturing the sheath with a quartz electrode, and applying gentle suction via a 7–10 MΩ saline-filled borosilicate electrode3. Although real-time PID monitoring in every trial controls for bulk stimulus waveform variability3, cross-fly differences in antennal positioning, surgical/collagenase state, or animal physiology can introduce baseline offsets and apparent temporal sharpening between unpaired OSN and PN PSTHs that do not originate from a single central synapse.  
Second, **peripheral ORN dynamics already account for step-onset timing, while uncalibrated static Olsen constants inflate the baseline and steady-state error**. Kim, Lazar, and Slutskiy (2015) established that Or59b OSNs already encode concentration rate of change3. As your benchmark tests indicate, feeding those OSN rates into the static Olsen equation already captures step-onset peaks (\~140 Hz) and temporal correlation (*r* ≈ 0.57), diverging primarily through an elevated baseline (29 Hz vs. 7 Hz) and 2.3× steady firing during odor (107 Hz vs. 45 Hz). Because Olsen, Bhandawat, and Wilson (2010) fitted their constants on VM7, DL5, and DM1 rather than DM44, uncalibrated static constants (*R*\_max and *σ*) can produce sustained overprediction independently of any missing dynamical filter.  
Third, **synaptic and inhibitory mechanisms vary substantially across glomeruli and cannot be transferred safely without DM4 validation**. Olsen, Bhandawat, and Wilson (2010) demonstrated that GABA\_A/GABA\_B antagonists increase PN gain in DM1 but not VM74; Kazama and Wilson (2008) showed that unitary ORN→PN currents co-vary with glomerular dendritic size and input resistance across VM7 and VM21; and Nagel, Hong, and Wilson (2015) fitted *f* \= 0.78 and *τ* \= 893 ms across DM6, VM2, VM7, and DL5—none of which is DM42. Importing parameters measured in other glomeruli violates glomerular specificity.  
Fourth, **candidate mechanisms operate on overlapping timescales and depend on unmeasured population inputs, creating severe non-identifiability**. Upstream ORN adaptation, homosynaptic STD, lateral presynaptic inhibition, and LN dynamics overlap dynamically across sub-second to second windows, and lateral presynaptic inhibition scales with total ORN activity across \~24 ORN types (![][image21])4—population activity that was not recorded in the single-channel Or59b/DM4 acetone experiments3. Tellingly, even Lazar, Liu, and Yeh's 23-parameter ODE model—requiring a heuristic 0.8 cap on ![][image18] and \>10⁶ parameter evaluations across affinity-scaled channels5—never exceeded \~70 Hz in your evaluation of the published example circuit rather than matching 150–190 Hz bursts. Without DM4 pharmacology (such as picrotoxin plus CGP54626) or direct ORN→PN stimulation, adding an unconstrained transient filter risks overfitting unpaired PSTHs rather than isolating true synaptic dynamics.
